extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy; citizens and theorists considering legitimacy, revolution, and the limits of political authority
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Locke's criteria for when a government is dissolved, when rulers breach their trust, and when people have a right to resist or erect a new legislative. Focuses on concrete triggers (altered elections, foreign subjection, neglect, invasion of property, corruption) and limits on lawful resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alteration of the legislative's use and exercise
rubrics_metrics.description: When the powers of the legislative are taken away or altered so as to deprive the society of the due exercise of their power; he who takes away the freedom, or hinders the acting of the legislative in its due seasons, in effect takes away the legislative, and puts an end to the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not mere change of names but alteration of the use and exercise of legislative powers dissolves government; emphasis on functional loss rather than formal titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitrary change of electors or methods of election
rubrics_metrics.description: When, by the arbitrary power of the prince, the electors, or ways of election, are altered, without the consent, and contrary to the common interest of the people, there also the legislative is altered: for, if others than those whom the society hath authorized thereunto, do chuse, or in another way than what the society hath prescribed, those chosen are not the legislative appointed by the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changing who elects or how elections occur (without consent/against common interest) substitutes a different legislative and therefore dissolves the existing government; the legitimacy of representatives depends on being chosen in the manner the society authorized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery of the people into subjection to a foreign power
rubrics_metrics.description: The delivery also of the people into the subjection of a foreign power, either by the prince, or by the legislative, is certainly a change of the legislative, and so a dissolution of the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loss of independence—being given over to another state's power—destroys the purpose of society (an intact, independent body governed by its own laws) and therefore dissolves government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Princely manipulation and use of state means to alter government
rubrics_metrics.description: The prince, having the force, treasure and offices of the state to employ...is in a condition to make great advances toward such changes, under pretence of lawful authority, and has it in his hands to terrify or suppress opposers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical explanation why the prince is often the agent of dissolution: control of coercive, financial, and administrative instruments enables covert or ostensible alteration of the legislative; warns against subtle legal pretexts and suppression of dissent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neglect or abandonment of executive functions (failure to execute laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: When he who has the supreme executive power, neglects and abandons that charge, so that the laws already made can no longer be put in execution. This is demonstratively to reduce all to anarchy, and so effectually to dissolve the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws exist to be executed; where execution ceases there is effectively no government. Lack of administration of justice or any remaining power to direct force/public necessities equals dissolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to erect a new legislative when government is dissolved
rubrics_metrics.description: When the government is dissolved, the people are at liberty to provide for themselves, by erecting a new legislative, differing from the other, by the change of persons, or form, or both, as they shall find it most for their safety and good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Society retains original right to preserve itself; people need not await total ruin. If old government is gone by oppression or foreign subjection, they may and should provide new institutions to secure safety and rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative (or prince) acting against trust by invading property or making arbitrary masters
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislative acts against the trust reposed in them, when they endeavour to invade the property of the subject, and to make themselves, or any part of the community, masters, or arbitrary disposers of the lives, liberties, or fortunes of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preservation of property is the reason men enter society; a legislature that seeks to destroy property or reduce people to slavery forfeits its trust and devolves power back to the people—this breach constitutes a state of war and dissolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive breach of trust by setting up arbitrary will or corrupting the representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: The supreme executor...acts against both [legislative and executive trust], when he goes about to set up his own arbitrary will as the law of the society...employs the force, treasure, and offices of the society, to corrupt the representatives, and gain them to his purposes; or openly preengages the electors, and prescribes to their choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrupting elections, controlling candidates, preengaging electors, or using state resources to make a compliant legislature is a fundamental breach of trust that undermines the people's fence for property and liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: People's right to judge whether trustees have breached their trust
rubrics_metrics.description: The people shall be judge; for who shall be judge whether his trustee or deputy acts well, and according to the trust reposed in him, but he who deputes him...he must, by having deputed him, have still a power to discard him, when he fails in his trust?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When no earthly judicature is competent or the matter is of great consequence, the body of the people is the proper judge of whether rulers have exceeded trust; if recourse to earthly judges is precluded, appeal may lie only to heaven and self-judgment in extreme cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance as self-defence permitted but revenge/punishment of superior forbidden
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-defence is a part of the law of nature; nor can it be denied the community, even against the king himself: but to revenge themselves upon him, must by no means be allowed them; it being not agreeable to that law...They may repulse the present attempt, but must not revenge past violences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permits defensive resistance to prevent imminent or designed injury, but prohibits using resistance as vengeance to punish a superior; defence is allowed insofar as it prevents the mischief, not for retribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance justified only against pervasive or design-based tyranny, not petty mismanagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Such revolutions happen not upon every little mismanagement...But if a long train of abuses, prevarications and artifices, all tending the same way, make the design visible to the people...they should then rouze themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes legitimate resistance from frivolous rebellion: isolated mistakes or occasional bad laws do not justify revolution; sustained, systemic, or deliberate designs to subvert rights do.

rubrics_metrics.name: Those who remove or change the legislative, and legislators who invade rights, are rebels
rubrics_metrics.description: They, who remove, or change the legislative, take away this decisive power...and so destroying the authority which the people did...they actually introduce a state of war...And if those, who by force take away the legislative, are rebels, the legislators themselves...can be no less esteemed so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both usurpers who violently replace the legitimate legislature and legitimate legislators who betray their trust by invading people's rights are culpable of rebellion and put themselves in a state of war with the people.

rubrics_metrics.name: State of war as cancelling former ties and justifying defensive punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Whosoever uses force without right...puts himself into a state of war with those against whom he so uses it; and in that state all former ties are cancelled, all other rights cease, and every one has a right to defend himself...he who opposes the unjust aggressor...has this superiority...to punish the offender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using force unjustly constitutes a state of war that dissolves previous obligations; the injured party may defend and, if prevailing, punish the offender to repair wrongs occasioned by the aggression (distinguishing defense from revenge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two specific cases where a king ceases to be king
rubrics_metrics.description: First: If he endeavour to overturn the government (e.g., resolves to ruin kingdom/commonwealth). Second: If a king makes himself the dependent of another and alienates his kingdom to a foreign power; in either case he ipso facto loses royal authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete thresholds for monarchical forfeiture of authority: (1) designs to destroy the commonwealth, (2) alienation/subjecting of the kingdom to foreign dominion; in such cases the king returns to the state of a private man and may be resisted like any aggressor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevention is preferable to waiting until oppression is irreversible
rubrics_metrics.description: To tell people they may provide for themselves, by erecting a new legislative, when by oppression, artifice, or being delivered over to a foreign power, their old one is gone, is only to tell them, they may expect relief when it is too late...they have not only a right to get out of it, but to prevent it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues against counsel to 'wait until the old legislature is fully destroyed'—people have the right to take preventive action before total subjection; otherwise the right is empty and mockery.
